title: External IDs, unique fields, matching rules, and duplicate rules
objectives: Define External ID and Unique using official custom-field attributes, including the shared 25-field cap.
Explain why upsert and API parent-child creates use External ID, not Name.
Separate matching rules (how records compare) from duplicate rules (what happens when they match).
Describe match keys as a performance pre-filter that narrows candidates before the matching equation.
diagnostic_question: An ERP will upsert Accounts, two users keep creating the same Contact, and leadership wants a warning for sales but a block for service. Which of External ID, Unique, matching rules, and duplicate rules do you configure first, and what would you not combine blindly?
definition: An External ID is a custom auto-number, email, number, or text field that stores an identifier from a system outside Salesforce and can be used to update or upsert via the API. Unique prevents duplicate values in that field (with case options on text). Matching rules define how records are compared; duplicate rules use those matching rules to warn, allow, or block. ([Custom Field Attributes](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.custom_field_attributes.htm); [Manage Duplicate Records](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.managing_duplicates_overview.htm))
why_it_matters: Without an External ID, nightly upserts become inserts and duplicates explode. Unique is a hard database constraint; matching rules are fuzzy comparison. Interviewers fail candidates who treat duplicate rules as the same thing as Unique, or who upsert on Name.
sixty_second_explanation: Think of passport control. External ID is the passport number issued by the traveler's home country—the other system. Unique means two travelers cannot hold the same passport number at this desk. A matching rule is how officers compare names, dates, and faces (exact or fuzzy). A duplicate rule is the policy: warn, let them through, or block the second person. Match keys are the first glance that narrows the line to the most likely look-alikes before the full comparison.
deeper_explanation: Custom Field Attributes: for each object that can have custom fields, you can set up to 25 custom auto-number, email, number, or text fields as External IDs. An External ID holds record identifiers from a system outside Salesforce. You can use it to update or upsert records using the API. When using the API or the Data Import Wizard for custom objects and solutions, you can use this field to prevent duplicates by also marking the field Unique. Custom fields marked Unique count against the same 25 External ID field limit. Custom indexing that Salesforce performs automatically in the background does not count against that limit. External ID is not available for external objects in the same way; each external object already has an External ID standard field. ([Custom Field Attributes](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.custom_field_attributes.htm))

Unique, if checked, prevents duplicate field values. For text, you choose whether ABC and abc are duplicates (case-insensitive) or different (case-sensitive). Help notes single-byte and double-byte versions of some punctuation are treated as identical for uniqueness, and superscript characters are not treated as unique (ABC² and ABC2 are identical). Unique is a constraint, not a fuzzy matcher. ([Custom Field Attributes](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.custom_field_attributes.htm))

Duplicate management finds and handles duplicates using matching rules plus duplicate rules. Duplicate rules and duplicate jobs specify matching rules that determine how duplicates are identified. Duplicate sets and reports list what was found. You can customize the UI (block versus warn, different rules per profile) and the comparison logic (custom fields, field mapping, matching criteria). Permissions: View Setup and Configuration to view rules; Customize Application to create, edit, activate, or deactivate them. ([Manage Duplicate Records](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.managing_duplicates_overview.htm))

Matching rules apply criteria and matching methods (normalization, match keys, algorithms). When a matching rule runs, it applies match key formulas first, narrowing to the 100 most likely duplicate records, then applies the matching equation only to those candidates. That is a performance design, not a promise that the 101st look-alike will be found. ([Things to Know About Matching Rules](https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sales.matching_rules_overview.htm))

mental_model.analogy: Passport control: External ID = home-country passport number, Unique = no two identical numbers at this desk, matching rule = how officers compare faces and names, duplicate rule = warn versus block, match keys = first glance that shortens the line.
useful_mapping: External ID → passport number from the other country/system
Unique → this desk will not file two identical numbers
Case-sensitive Unique → ABC and abc are different passports
matching rule → comparison method (exact/fuzzy, which fields)
match keys → first-pass shortlist (documented as the 100 most likely)
duplicate rule → policy when a match is found (alert, allow, block, report)
duplicate job → sweep of records already in the hall, not only new arrivals
upsert → 'if this passport exists, update that traveler; else enroll'
where_it_breaks: Unique is exact on one field; matching rules can be fuzzy across several fields.
Match keys can miss a duplicate that is not in the top 100 candidates.
External ID does not by itself block UI duplicates unless Unique or a duplicate rule also applies.
The analogy does not encode encryption, deterministic matching, or Experience Cloud users.

teach_back_prompt: Explain External ID versus Unique versus matching rules versus duplicate rules to a BA, then name one place the passport-control analogy breaks.

interview_explanation.thirty_seconds: External ID stores the other system's key for upsert. Unique is an exact no-duplicates constraint and counts toward the 25 External ID fields. Matching rules compare records, including fuzzy methods. Duplicate rules decide warn, allow, or block using those matching rules.
interview_explanation.two_minutes: I split constraint, comparison, and policy. Integration: External ID, usually Unique so upsert cannot collide. UI twins: matching rule plus duplicate rule, maybe different actions per profile. Existing mess: duplicate job, not only save-time rules. I mention match keys shortlist about 100 candidates so I do not promise perfect recall. I never say Unique is a matching rule, and I never upsert on Name.

terminology.plain: A field that stores the other system's record key so APIs can find the row without a Salesforce Id.
terminology.precise: Up to 25 custom auto-number, email, number, or text External ID fields per eligible object. Used to update or upsert via the API (and can help Wizard/API duplicate prevention when also Unique).
terminology.example: LAB_ERP_Id__c on Account, used by Data Loader upsert.
terminology.non_example: Account Name, which is not an External ID unless you misuse it.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Salesforce Id: the platform's own primary key, not the vendor key.
terminology.boundary: External objects' standard External ID field is a different model.

terminology.plain: A field setting that rejects a second row with the same value.
terminology.precise: Prevents duplicate field values. Text can be case-sensitive or not. Unique custom fields count against the 25 External ID limit even if you did not also tick External ID.
terminology.example: LAB_ERP_Id__c Unique so two Accounts cannot share an ERP key.
terminology.non_example: A matching rule on First Name + Last Name + Email, which can be fuzzy and is not a Unique checkbox.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: Duplicate rule: policy after a match, not a single-field database uniqueness constraint.
terminology.boundary: Help's character-normalization notes (single-byte vs double-byte, superscripts) matter for messy imports.

terminology.plain: The definition of how two records are compared.
terminology.precise: Applies matching criteria, methods, algorithms, normalization, and match keys. Standard rules ship with predefined criteria; custom rules let you choose fields and methods.
terminology.example: Standard Contact matching on name and email versus a custom rule that includes LAB_MemberId__c.
terminology.non_example: The Unique checkbox on one field.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: duplicate rule: consumes a matching rule and decides the user/API outcome.
terminology.boundary: Encryption: matching on Shield fields needs deterministic encryption (neighboring security topic).

terminology.plain: A first-pass fingerprint that shortlists likely duplicates before the full compare.
terminology.precise: Help: match keys increase duplicate-rule performance by a preliminary comparison that narrows to the 100 most likely duplicate records; then the matching equation runs on those rows.
terminology.example: Normalized email/name keys that pull 100 candidates before fuzzy scoring.
terminology.non_example: The 25 External ID field limit, which is unrelated to match keys.
terminology.confusable_neighbor: External ID: an integration key, not a matching-rule match key.
terminology.boundary: A duplicate outside the shortlist can be missed—say so in interviews.

terminology.plain: The policy for what happens when a matching rule finds a duplicate.
terminology.precise: Duplicate rules specify matching rules and how to handle matches (Help examples: block create, warn, vary by profile). They are metadata you activate in Setup.
terminology.example: Sales profile sees an alert; integration user is blocked on Account create.
terminology.non_example: A validation rule that checks a single amount field (DQM-004).
terminology.confusable_neighbor: duplicate job: finds existing duplicates using matching rules, not only on save.
terminology.boundary: Merge of the resulting sets is a neighboring user action, not this lesson's full merge topic.

terminology.plain: A sweep that looks for duplicates already stored, not just the record being saved.
terminology.precise: Help lists duplicate jobs alongside duplicate rules as the things that specify matching rules and produce duplicate sets and reports.
terminology.example: Run a Contact duplicate job after a Wizard import to list pairs.
terminology.non_example: A nightly upsert, which is a load operation (DQM-002).
terminology.boundary: Job volume and object support: Needs verification in the org.

when_to_use: When an integration must upsert on External IDs instead of Salesforce Ids or Name.
When Unique fields are required so two records cannot share the same integration key, and you must count that toward the 25 External ID fields.
When matching rules should define fuzzy or multi-field comparison and duplicate rules should warn or block.
When a duplicate job must sweep existing records after an import, not only intercept the next save.
When an interviewer asks how match keys narrow candidates before the matching equation.
when_not_to_use: Do not use Unique as a substitute for matching rules when the business needs fuzzy name-and-email comparison.
Do not use a duplicate rule as the External ID for Data Loader upsert—the upsert key is a field attribute.
Do not mark every text field External ID; the object cap is 25 and Unique shares that budget.
Do not promise matching rules will find every possible twin; match keys shortlist the 100 most likely records.
Do not test duplicate rules by creating real customer twins in production.

decision_table.choose: Custom External ID, usually Unique, and upsert on that field.
decision_table.not: Insert plus hope, or upsert on Name.

decision_table.not: A matching rule alone, which is comparison rather than a uniqueness constraint.

interview_questions.question: What is an External ID, and why do integrations care?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: A custom auto-number, email, number, or text field—up to 25 per object—that stores the other system's key so API or Data Loader upsert can find the row without a Salesforce Id.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I quote Custom Field Attributes: outside identifier, update/upsert via API. I usually also mark Unique so two Accounts cannot share the ERP key, and I mention Unique consumes the same 25-field budget. I never upsert on Name. I distinguish Salesforce Id (platform) from External ID (vendor). External objects' standard External ID is a different model; I do not mix it in unless asked.
interview_questions.example: LAB_ERP_Id__c on Account; nightly upsert updates the same Id.
tradeoffs: Unique fail-closed vs allowing key reuse

interview_questions.question: Unique versus matching rules versus duplicate rules?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Unique is an exact field constraint. Matching rules define how records compare, including fuzzy methods. Duplicate rules use matching rules and decide warn, allow, or block.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I draw three boxes: constraint, comparison, policy. Unique counts toward External ID limits. Matching has criteria, methods, match keys. Duplicate rules can differ by profile. A duplicate job uses matching rules on data already stored. I refuse 'we turned on Unique on LastName' as a fuzzy-dedupe strategy.
interview_questions.example: Unique on LAB_ERP_Id__c; matching on name+email; sales warned, service blocked.
weak_answer_warnings: Treating all three as one checkbox

interview_questions.question: Upsert created a second Account with the same ERP key. Diagnose.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: The field was not External ID, not mapped, the job was insert, or Unique was off and the match missed. Fix the field attributes and the operation, then merge or delete the extra LAB_ row in sandbox.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I inspect the field, the mapping, and process.operation. Data Loader upsert only matches a custom external ID. Duplicate rules might have allowed the second row if Unique was off. I do not 'fix' it by matching on Name going forward. After the field is correct, I plan a one-time cleanup (DQM-002 delete/merge) and a duplicate job to list leftovers.
interview_questions.example: CSV column ERP_KEY mapped to Account Number instead of LAB_ERP_Id__c.
follow_ups: Would Unique have blocked the second row?
How do you prevent the next load?

interview_questions.question: A pair of Contacts looks identical but no duplicate alert fired. What official limit do you mention?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Match keys first shortlist the 100 most likely records; the matching equation runs on that set. A twin outside the shortlist can be missed. Then I check if rules are active and in-profile.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I do not invent a match score. I walk Help's two-stage design: keys, then equation. I look at normalization, selected fields, and whether we needed a custom matching rule. I consider a duplicate job for existing rows. I also check the action is alert versus silent allow. I never promise 100% detection.
interview_questions.example: Two LAB_ Contacts with swapped emails that did not share a match key.
follow_ups: When do you add a custom field to the matching rule?

interview_questions.question: How would you let sales proceed on a duplicate and stop service?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: One matching rule, then duplicate-rule handling customized by profile—Help explicitly lists different rules or actions for different profiles, including block versus warn.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I keep comparison logic in the matching rule so both teams share a definition of 'same person.' Policy lives in duplicate rules. I test both profiles in sandbox. I mention API users as a third persona: blocking them may be correct for UI twins but must not break a legitimate External ID upsert—Needs verification of the rule's operation and user-scope settings in that org.
interview_questions.example: LAB_Sales alert; LAB_Service block on Contact create.
tradeoffs: API integration user vs human profiles
weak_answer_warnings: Two different matching definitions of the same person

interview_questions.question: You are out of External ID slots but need another Unique email. What do you recall from Help?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Unique custom fields count against the 25 External ID fields. I audit unused External ID and Unique flags before adding another. Automatic background indexes do not consume that cap.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I list fields with External ID or Unique. I drop unused flags. I do not confuse platform auto-indexes with this budget. If we truly need more integration keys, I escalate—I do not invent a higher unofficial cap. I also ask whether the new email should be a matching-rule field instead of Unique.
interview_questions.example: Twelve leftover Unique checkboxes on unused LAB_ fields blocking a new ERP key.
follow_ups: Which types can be External ID?

interview_questions.question: Why not just make Account Name Unique and skip External ID?
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: Names collide and change. External ID is the outside system's identifier for upsert. Unique on Name would block legitimate same-name accounts and still would not give the ERP a stable key.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I separate human labels from integration keys. Unique on Name is the wrong constraint for companies that share names. Matching rules handle people-shaped similarity. Upsert documented against a custom external ID. If they want no two Accounts with the same ERP key, Unique belongs on that External ID field, which also spends the 25-field budget honestly.
interview_questions.example: Two 'Acme' customers in different cities; one ERP key each.
tradeoffs: Human-readable Name vs stable vendor key
weak_answer_warnings: Agreeing to Unique on Name as the integration strategy

interview_questions.question: Teach the passport-control analogy and where it breaks.
interview_questions.answer_30_seconds: External ID is the home-country passport number, Unique is no two identical numbers, matching is how officers compare faces, duplicate rules are warn versus block. It breaks because match keys only shortlist about 100 travelers, so a twin can be missed.
interview_questions.answer_2_minutes: I map upsert to 'update this passport holder or enroll.' I map duplicate jobs to a sweep of people already in the hall. I break the analogy: Unique is not fuzzy; matching is not a database unique index; External ID alone does not stop UI name twins; encryption can disable matching unless deterministic. I avoid library or drawer language.
interview_questions.example: Teaching a BA why sales can be warned while the ERP upsert uses a passport number field.
